bodyHtml:
This final chapter pulls the track together. First, three worked case studies on illustrative ES sessions, each read through the profile, the order flow and the liquidity framework together. Then the playbook: a 16-point checklist that turns the whole track into a routine you can follow every session.

The cases are hypothetical and built to show the reading process clearly. Real sessions are messier. The point is the questions you ask and the order you ask them in, not the specific outcomes. Nothing here shows or implies a trading result.

Case 1: open inside value, a rotation day

Pre-session map. Yesterday was D-shaped: POC 5,307.00, value area 5,303.00 to 5,309.00. No tails, no poor extremes. Value has overlapped for two days in a row, so the market is in balance.

Reading. The open is inside value, so the first-hour question is whether it stays there. Bar 2 probes toward VAL and bar 3 closes back up: a responsive buyer at the lower edge. Bars 4 and 5 rotate up to VAH and slightly beyond, and bar 6 turns back. Neither edge is accepted. On the footprint, a trader would expect to see the extremes of bars 2 and 5 printing on shrinking aggressive volume, the exhaustion pattern from VP-09.

Lesson. On a balance day the value-area edges are where responsive trade happens, and the POC is where the market returns. Initiative trades that bet on a breakout from value are the ones most likely to fail on this kind of day. It is also the kind of day where doing nothing is often the right call: a rotation inside a range you already mapped offers few clear moments of evidence.

Case 2: open above the range, acceptance

Pre-session map. Same prior profile. Overnight, price moved above yesterday's high at 5,315.00. The market opens above the whole prior range.

Reading. An open outside the prior range poses a sharp question: accepted or rejected? The first pullback (bar 3) holds at 5,318.75 without getting anywhere near yesterday's value. Each later bar makes a higher high and holds a higher low. On the profile, the developing POC would move up with price, which is value following price. On the footprint, pullbacks would show light selling and buy imbalances on the way back up. VWAP sits under price all session. Everything points the same way: this is initiative buying being accepted.

Lesson. Case 1 and Case 2 used the same prior profile. What differed was where the market opened and whether the new prices were accepted. Selling "expensive" prices on a day like this is fading a trend (VP-04). For an SMC trader, the equivalent read is a bullish daily bias with structure making higher highs and no reason to look for shorts.

Case 3: a poke through a poor high

Pre-session map. Yesterday closed with a poor high at 5,315.75: several periods stopped at the same price, with no tail. In core-course terms, that is a set of equal highs with buy-side liquidity above them (chapter 07).

Reading. Bar 1 rallies into the poor high on positive delta (+61). Bar 2 trades through it by two ticks, and the top rows show aggressive buying: that is the breakout buying and stop orders being triggered. Then it closes back below the level with delta -160, and sell imbalances stack on the way down. The buyers who bought the break are now trapped. Liquidity framework: a sweep of the equal highs. Profile framework: the poor high has been "repaired", and the auction up there is now finished. Order flow: trapped buyers and selling taking over. Three methods agree.

Lesson. This is the combined read from VP-11 in its cleanest form. Note what would have cancelled it: bar 2 closing above the level and bar 3 holding there. That is the condition to write in the plan before the session, and it is where the risk of the idea is defined.

The playbook checklist

Each section opens and closes; the first is open by default. The references point to the chapter that covers each step.

Before the session (5)
  1. Data: contract, session (RTH/ETH), volume type and delta method confirmed (VP-10).
  2. Yesterday: POC, VAH, VAL, tails, poor highs/lows marked (VP-02, VP-03).
  3. Context: composite value, naked POCs, value migration noted (VP-05).
  4. Liquidity: equal highs/lows and old swing points marked (ch 07).
  5. Scenarios: one bullish and one bearish plan, each with its invalidation, written down.
At the open (3)
  1. Open location: inside value, outside value inside range, or outside range.
  2. Initial balance size compared with recent days (VP-02).
  3. VWAP position and first range extension (VP-04, VP-06).
At a level (5)
  1. Is price reaching a level you marked before the session?
  2. Profile: is it building volume there (acceptance) or rejecting it quickly?
  3. Footprint: absorption, exhaustion, imbalances, trapped traders (VP-09)?
  4. Liquidity: is this a sweep of a marked pool (ch 12, VP-11)?
  5. Risk: size and stop from your risk plan, not from the pattern (ch 36).
After the session (3)
  1. Journal the day type, open location and what each level did.
  2. Screenshot the profile and the footprint at each decision.
  3. Update naked POCs and the value-migration log.

The checklist is deliberately short. It does not tell you when to trade. It makes sure that when you do, you have looked at the same things in the same order as last time. That consistency is what makes the journal useful: if you change the process every day, you can't tell whether a result came from the method or from the change.

Building your own version

Take this checklist and cut it down to what you actually use. If you trade from the liquidity framework and use the profile only as a filter, the "at a level" section may be all you need during the session. If you are primarily an order-flow trader, you may add items, such as a baseline of typical volume per half hour. Put your version at the top of your playbook from the core course (chapter 34, chapter 35) and review it monthly.

A good test of a checklist item is whether you can answer it with a yes, a no, or a price. "Is the market strong?" fails that test. "Is price above VWAP?" and "Where is yesterday's VAL?" pass it. Items that can't be answered quickly get skipped under pressure, so rewrite them until they can.

A journal entry template

The checklist tells you what to look at; the journal records what you saw. A short, consistent entry after each session is enough. This template mirrors the checklist so the two stay in step.

Data setup

What to write: Contract, session, delta method.

Example (Case 3): ES front month, RTH, exchange bid/ask delta.

Prior profile

What to write: Shape, POC, value area, tails, poor extremes.

Example (Case 3): Poor high at the top of yesterday's range.

Open location

What to write: Inside value, outside value, outside range.

Example (Case 3): Inside the prior range, below the poor high.

Day type (provisional, then final)

What to write: From the IB and range extension.

Example (Case 3): Normal variation, then neutral by the close.

Levels reached

What to write: Which marked levels traded and what happened.

Example (Case 3): Poor high: poked through two ticks, closed back below.

Order-flow evidence

What to write: The pattern names from VP-09, or "none".

Example (Case 3): Trapped buyers, stacked sell imbalances.

Scenario result

What to write: Which written scenario played out, if any.

Example (Case 3): Bearish scenario; the cancel condition was never met.

Process notes

What to write: Items skipped, rules broken, questions.

Example (Case 3): Checked VWAP late; move it earlier in the list.

After a month you will have twenty or so entries. Sort them by open location and by day type, and look at what your marked levels did in each group. That is your own evidence about how these methods behave on your instrument, built from sessions you actually watched. It is worth far more than any rule of thumb in a book, including this one.

How the track fits together

Looking back over the twelve chapters, the track builds one idea at a time.

  1. Why price moves (VP-01): markets auction for value, alternating between balance and imbalance.
  2. Where value is (VP-02 to VP-06): TPO letters, volume profiles, shapes, day types, composites and VWAP all measure it.
  3. How trades happen (VP-07 to VP-09): orders, the book, matching, and the footprint patterns that record them.
  4. Whether the data is real (VP-10): futures volume versus tick volume, and how your platform classifies trades.
  5. How it fits Stryker's framework (VP-11 and this chapter): liquidity, structure and imbalance, checked against value and order flow.

If a part feels shaky, go back to its chapter and redo the practice exercises on fresh sessions. The exercises matter more than the reading.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping the pre-session map. Without marked levels, order flow at random prices is noise.
  • Using every tool every time. The checklist is a menu with a fixed order, not a requirement to find every pattern.
  • Letting the pattern set the stop. Risk comes from your plan and account (chapter 36).
  • Reviewing only losing days. Review the process on every day, including the ones you didn't trade.
  • Treating these case studies as templates. They show a way of reading, not setups that will repeat.

Key takeaways

  • The same prior profile can lead to a rotation day or a trend day. The open and acceptance decide which.
  • The strongest reads come from independent methods agreeing at a level marked in advance.
  • Every scenario needs a written condition that would prove it wrong.
  • A short, fixed checklist makes your journal meaningful.

Practice exercises

  1. Find a real ES session that matches each case (rotation inside value, accepted open outside range, failed break of a poor high). Write each one up in the same format.
  2. Use the checklist for ten sessions in a simulator without taking trades. Note which items you skipped and why.
  3. Cut the checklist down to the ten items you actually use and add it to your playbook.
  4. After twenty sessions, count how often your pre-session scenarios matched what happened and what was different when they didn't.

Self-check quiz

1. Case 1 and Case 2 had the same prior profile. What made them different?

Where the market opened and whether the new prices were accepted.

2. In Case 2, what showed acceptance?

The first pullback held far above prior value, and each bar built higher with value following price.

3. In Case 3, which three methods agreed?

Liquidity (sweep of equal highs), profile (the poor high repaired, auction finished), and order flow (trapped buyers, sell imbalances).

4. What would have cancelled the Case 3 reading?

Bar 2 closing above the poor high and the next bar holding there.

5. What makes a good checklist item?

One you can answer quickly with a yes, a no, or a price.

Sources

  1. Volume profile indicators: basic concepts - TradingView Help Center
  2. Time price opportunity charts explained - TradingView Help Center
  3. Volume Footprint charts: a complete guide - TradingView Help Center
  4. Order Flow Volumetric Bars - NinjaTrader 8 Help Guide
  5. Market profile - Wikipedia
  6. Mind Over Markets, Updated Edition (Dalton, Jones, Dalton; Wiley 2013) - further reading
